newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian PM urges united front against crime.
newsitem.headline: Russian PM urges united front against crime.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin called on Friday for a united front to fight crime and said that up to half the economy may have fallen into an unofficial or illegal "grey zone".
He said police had failed to conquer crime which had reached such a level that ordinary Russians lived in fear and state security was under threat.
"The main question today is can the authorities curb the rise of crime in vitally important areas of society," Chernomyrdin said in a speech to interior ministry officials.
"For this we must consolidate the healthy forces in society in the search for a way out of the crime crisis and create a united front to resist the rise in crime."

Corruption is rife in Russia and violent crime has risen sharply since communist rule ended in 1991, with mafia-style gangs emerging and gangland killings becoming common. Victims include businessmen, politicians and media figures.
"Crime today is a factor which really poses a threat to state security," Chernomyrdin told a meeting at which Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov outlined the ministry's plans for 1997.
"None of the other problems facing our country can be ranked with the problem of crime."

In a sign of the extent to which crime has affected Russian society, Chernomyrdin said that from one-fifth to half of Russia's economy was now in the "grey zone" -- the untaxed and unofficial shadow economy.

"Estimates vary between 20 and 50 percent, and this does not simply mean tax evasion," he said. "The shadow economy is a breeding ground for corruption and money-laundering, a source for further criminality, criminals and organised crime."
Chernomyrdin said criminal groups were using false foreign trade contracts with artificially lowered prices and exports of raw materials had gone out of control.
"The scale of economic crimes requires a immediate reaction from all government and non-government institutions."
He called for a system to be worked out to tighten checks on capital movements, property transactions and investment and said parliament should accelerate work to pass a new criminal code.
"Crime without punishment discredits the idea of a law-abiding state because people start to think the law can be violated with impunity. The criminal belongs behind bars," Chernomyrdin said.

Kulikov said this week that Russia had registered 2.2 million crimes since the start of the year, just over 100,000 fewer than in the same period in 1995. Some 71 percent had been solved within 10 months, he said.
But he told Friday's meeting there had been no breakthrough. "There are dozens of major criminal gangs," he said.
